summary: Tretort Linen Holdings, LLC (client, Buyer) signed a Stock Purchase Agreement on July 20, 2026 to buy all outstanding stock of Pelmont Textile Care, Inc., a commercial laundry and linen-rental company serving hospitals and hotels, from Drusisk Holdings, Inc. (Seller). The price is $48,500,000, funded partly by a $6,000,000 Seller Note and a $4,850,000 indemnity escrow. Closing is pending, with an Outside Date of December 31, 2026. The folder holds the signed SPA, the closing-form escrow agreement, Seller Note and TSA, a 2021 IP assignment under which the founder assigned Pelmont's wash-chemistry formulas and dosing software, a side letter, the Buyer's board consent, the LOI, the plant office lease and an equipment service agreement. The six planted issues are: (1) an unaddressed change-of-control reacquisition right in the IP assignment; (2) a missed environmental objection window measured against dates in the board consent; (3) a narrower definition of 'Losses' in the Seller Note that controls set-off; (4) New York law and forum in the escrow agreement against Delaware in the SPA; (5) a general survival period that runs out before a claims bar lifts; and (6) unrestricted assignment by the Seller-provider under the TSA.

parties.name: Drusisk Holdings, Inc.

parties.name: Pelmont Textile Care, Inc.

15 Business Days after Seller delivers the Phase I Report

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Section 8.3 of the 2021 IP Assignment Agreement (D2) is between Odile Fenwright and the Company. It lets Fenwright reacquire the Assigned IP for $1 if the Company undergoes a Change of Control without her prior written consent. The Assigned IP is the Company's proprietary wash-chemistry formulas and dosing software. Change of Control there means any transfer of more than 50% of the Company's voting stock, which the stock sale clearly is. The SPA (D1) does not address this. Section 1.1 defines 'Required Consents' as only the consents listed in Section 7.2(d). Section 7.2(d) lists only an estoppel certificate from the Landlord. Section 6.4 obliges Seller to obtain only the Required Consents. Read together, closing as drafted triggers Fenwright's reacquisition right with no closing condition or covenant requiring her consent. The office lease (D9) does not cure this; it concerns the landlord only.
issues.expected_finding: The stock sale is a Change of Control under Section 8.3 of the IP Assignment Agreement, which lets Fenwright reacquire the Company's core wash-chemistry and dosing IP for $1. The SPA's Required Consents (Sections 1.1, 6.4 and 7.2(d)) omit her consent, so Buyer should add Fenwright's written consent and waiver as a Required Consent and closing condition before closing.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: SPA Section 6.7 (D1) requires Buyer to deliver an Environmental Objection Notice within fifteen (15) Business Days after Seller delivers the Phase I Report. If Buyer does not, it is deemed to have accepted the environmental conditions identified in the report and waives indemnity for them under Section 9.2(d). The report concerns, for example, historical perchloroethylene use at the plant. The Buyer's board consent (D7) records in its recitals that Seller delivered the Phase I Report on August 3, 2026, a Monday. It also records that Buyer's officers delivered the Environmental Objection Notice on September 4, 2026. Fifteen Business Days from August 3, 2026 ends on August 24, 2026, with no intervening holidays, so the notice was eleven days late. The board consent resolves that Buyer disputes any deemed acceptance and reserves all rights. That shows Buyer has not accepted the result and the point remains open to negotiation before closing.
detect_terms: fifteen (15) Business Days after Seller delivers the Phase I Report
issues.expected_finding: Buyer's Environmental Objection Notice of September 4, 2026 came after the window under SPA Section 6.7 closed on August 24, 2026 (15 Business Days after the August 3, 2026 Phase I delivery recorded in the board consent). Seller can therefore argue Buyer accepted the Phase I conditions and waived the Section 9.2(d) environmental indemnity for them, so Buyer should obtain a written waiver or amendment from Seller before closing confirming the notice is effective.

issues.label: defined term inconsistency
issues.description: SPA Section 1.1 (D1) defines 'Losses' broadly: damages, diminution in value, reasonable attorneys' fees and environmental remediation costs. SPA Section 9.6 lets Buyer set off the amount of any Losses against principal and interest under the Seller Note. The Seller Note (D4) defines 'Losses' in Section 1 for all purposes of the note. That definition covers only out-of-pocket damages finally awarded by a non-appealable judgment, excluding attorneys' fees, environmental remediation costs and diminution in value. Note Section 5 limits Maker's set-off to 'Losses'. Under SPA Section 11.12, each Ancillary Agreement controls matters it specifically governs, so the note's narrow definition governs set-off. Buyer therefore cannot set off agreed or unadjudicated indemnity amounts, fees or remediation costs, and must keep paying Seller while litigating.
detect_terms: finally awarded by a non-appealable judgment
issues.expected_finding: Because SPA Section 11.12 lets the Seller Note control set-off, the note's narrow definition of 'Losses' (judgment-only, excluding attorneys' fees, remediation costs and diminution in value) overrides the broad SPA definition, gutting Buyer's Section 9.6 set-off right. The note should be conformed to use the SPA definition of Losses and permit set-off of claimed amounts pending resolution.
detect_terms2: set off the amount of any Losses

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: Section 12.6 of the Escrow Agreement (D3) chooses the laws of the State of New York and submits all disputes under it to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in the Borough of Manhattan. SPA Sections 11.8 and 11.9 (D1) choose Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the Delaware Court of Chancery. Under SPA Section 11.12, each Ancillary Agreement controls matters it specifically governs, so disputes over release of the $4,850,000 escrow go to New York. The underlying indemnity claims go to Delaware Chancery. Buyer faces split proceedings, inconsistent rulings and a Seller able to contest escrow release in a different forum from the merits.
detect_terms: laws of the State of New York
issues.expected_finding: The Escrow Agreement's New York law and exclusive Manhattan forum conflict with the SPA's Delaware law and exclusive Chancery forum. Under SPA Section 11.12 the escrow clause controls escrow disputes, splitting indemnity and escrow-release litigation, so the Escrow Agreement should be conformed to Delaware law and the Court of Chancery (or expressly defer escrow-release disputes to the SPA forum) before it is signed at closing.

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: SPA Section 9.1 (D1) provides that the General Representations survive until nine (9) months after the Closing Date. The General Representations include Section 4.7 (Financial Statements) and Section 4.12 (Customer Contracts and Rebates). Claims must be noticed before that expiry. SPA Section 9.4(c) bars any claim for breach of Sections 4.7 or 4.12 until Buyer delivers audited financial statements of the Company for the first full fiscal year beginning after the Closing Date. Those statements are due within 120 days after the December 31 fiscal year end. For any closing on or before the December 31, 2026 Outside Date, the first full fiscal year runs through December 31, 2027 and the audit falls in 2028. That is well after the nine-month survival period expires in 2027. Read together, the two provisions make claims under Sections 4.7 and 4.12 impossible to bring in time. The nine-month period also departs from the 18 months in the LOI (D8).
detect_terms: nine (9) months after the Closing Date
first full fiscal year beginning after the Closing Date
issues.expected_finding: The nine-month survival in SPA Section 9.1 expires before the Section 9.4(c) bar on financial-statement and customer-contract claims lifts (audited statements for the first full post-closing fiscal year, due in 2028). Buyer would have no usable indemnity for breaches of Sections 4.7 and 4.12, so survival should be extended to at least the 18 months agreed in the LOI and the claims bar removed or survival tolled until it lifts.

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description: Section 11.3 of the Transition Services Agreement (D5) provides that Provider (Drusisk Holdings, Inc.) may assign this Agreement or delegate any Services, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Recipient (the Company). Recipient may not assign without Provider's consent. The services are billing, route dispatch and customer-portal hosting, and they give the provider full access to the Company's hospital and hotel customer lists, pricing and route data. Nothing stops Seller from assigning to or subcontracting with a competing laundry operator. SPA Section 11.3's assignment restriction covers only the SPA itself, and under SPA Section 11.12 the TSA controls its own assignment.
issues.expected_finding: TSA Section 11.3 lets Seller assign the TSA or delegate services to anyone, including a competing laundry operator that would then receive the Company's customer, pricing and route data. The TSA should be revised before closing to require Recipient's prior written consent for any assignment or subcontracting by Provider and to bar assignment to competitors.
